paragraphs: Most of the evils and vices that make this world so dreary a scene to the reflective mind flow from the respect paid to property, as from a poisoned fountain. For it is in the most polished society that loathsome reptiles and venomous serpents lurk beneath the rank undergrowth; and there, too, is a sensuality pampered by the still, sultry air, which saps every good disposition before it can ripen into virtue.

One class presses upon another, for all are trying to win respect on account of their property; and property, once gained, will win the respect that is due only to talents and virtue. Men neglect the duties that fall upon them as men, yet are treated like demigods. Religion, too, is separated from morality by a ceremonial veil, and yet men wonder that the world is almost, quite literally, a den of swindlers or oppressors.

A homely proverb speaks a shrewd truth: the devil will find work for anyone he finds idle. And what can hereditary wealth and titles produce except habitual idleness? For man is so made that he can learn the proper use of his faculties only by exercising them, and he will not exercise them unless necessity of some kind first sets the wheels in motion. Likewise, virtue can be acquired only by carrying out our duties to one another; but a being who is coaxed out of his humanity by the flattery of hangers-on will scarcely feel the importance of these sacred duties. Society must establish more equality, or morality will never gain ground; and this virtuous equality will not stand firm even if it is founded on a rock, so long as one half of mankind is chained by fate to its base, for they will keep undermining it through ignorance or pride. It is useless to expect virtue from women until they are, to some degree, independent of men; indeed, it is useless to expect even that strength of natural affection which would make them good wives and good mothers. While they are wholly dependent on their husbands they will be cunning, base and selfish; and the men who can be gratified by the fawning, doting devotion of a spaniel have little delicacy. For love cannot be bought, in any sense of the word: its silken wings shrivel at once when anything other than a return in kind is sought. Yet while wealth makes men feeble, and women live, as it were, by their personal charms, how can we expect them to carry out those ennobling duties which demand both effort and self-denial? Hereditary property corrupts the mind with false refinement. Its unfortunate victims, swaddled from birth, if I may put it so, seldom use the power of moving either body or mind; and so, seeing everything through a single medium, and a false one, they cannot discern what true merit and happiness consist in. False indeed must that light be when the trappings of rank hide the man and make him stalk about in masquerade, dragging from one scene of dissipation to the next his nerveless limbs, which hang in stupid listlessness, and rolling about that vacant eye which tells us plainly that there is no mind at home.

What I mean to conclude, therefore, is that a society is not properly organized if it does not compel men and women to carry out their respective duties by making that the only way to earn the approval of their fellow creatures, which every human being wishes to gain somehow. It follows that the respect paid to wealth and to mere personal charms is a true north-east wind, which withers the tender blossoms of affection and virtue. Nature has wisely attached affections to duties, to sweeten toil and to give the efforts of reason that vigour which only the heart can give. But affection that is merely put on, because it is the badge assigned to a certain role, while the duties of that role go unfulfilled, is one of the empty compliments that vice and folly are obliged to pay to virtue and to the real nature of things.

To illustrate my opinion, I need only point out this: when a woman is admired for her beauty and lets herself become so intoxicated by the admiration she receives that she neglects the indispensable duty of a mother, she sins against herself, by failing to cultivate an affection that would make her both useful and happy. True happiness, by which I mean all the contentment and virtuous satisfaction that can be snatched in this imperfect state, must arise from well-regulated affections; and every affection includes a duty. Men do not see the misery they cause, and the vicious weakness they foster, by urging women only to make themselves pleasing. They do not consider that in this way they set natural and artificial duties in conflict, sacrificing the comfort and respectability of a woman’s life to sensual notions of beauty, when in nature all these things are in harmony.

Cold would be the heart of a husband, unless early debauchery had made him unnatural, who did not feel more delight at seeing his child nursed at its mother’s breast than the most artful wanton tricks could ever arouse. Yet wealth leads women to scorn this natural way of strengthening the marriage bond and of entwining esteem with more tender memories. To keep their beauty, and to wear the flowery crown of the day that gives them a kind of right to reign for a short while over the sex, they neglect to stamp impressions on their husbands’ hearts that would be remembered with more tenderness than even their maiden charms, when the snow on the head began to chill the breast. The maternal care of a reasonable, affectionate woman is deeply moving; and the chastened dignity with which a mother returns the caresses that she and her child receive from a father who has been carrying out the serious duties of his position is not only a respectable sight but a beautiful one. Indeed, so peculiar are my feelings (and I have tried not to catch artificial ones) that, after being wearied by the sight of insipid grandeur and of the slavish ceremonies that, with cumbersome pomp, took the place of domestic affection, I have turned to some other scene to relieve my eye by resting it on the refreshing green that nature scatters everywhere. I have then watched with pleasure a woman nursing her children and carrying out the duties of her position with, perhaps, only one servant to take the menial part of the housework off her hands. I have seen her make herself and her children ready, with no luxury but cleanliness, to receive her husband, who, coming home weary in the evening, found smiling babies and a clean hearth. My heart has lingered in the midst of that group, and has even throbbed with shared emotion when the scrape of the well-known footstep raised a pleasant stir.

While my benevolence has been gratified by contemplating this unaffected picture, I have thought that a couple of this kind, equally necessary to each other and equally independent, because each carried out the duties belonging to their station, possessed everything that life could give. They were raised far enough above abject poverty not to have to weigh the importance of every farthing they spent, and they had enough to spare them from a chilly system of economy that narrows both heart and mind. I declare, so common are my notions, that I do not know what else would be needed to make this the happiest as well as the most respectable situation in the world, except a taste for literature, to bring a little variety and interest into conversation, and some spare money to give to the needy and to buy books. For when the heart is opened by compassion, and the head is busy arranging useful plans, it is not pleasant to have a prim little imp constantly tugging back one’s elbow to stop the hand from drawing out an almost empty purse, while whispering some prudent maxim about justice coming first.

Yet destructive as riches and inherited honours are to human character, they debase and cramp women, if possible, even more than men, because men may still to some degree develop their faculties by becoming soldiers and statesmen.

As soldiers, I grant, they can now for the most part gather only vainglorious laurels, while they adjust the European balance of power to a hair, taking particular care that no bleak northern nook or strait should tip the scale. But the days of true heroism are over, when a citizen fought for his country like a Fabricius or a Washington and then went back to his farm, to let his virtuous ardour flow in a calmer but no less wholesome stream. No, our British heroes are more often sent from the gaming table than from the plough; and their passions have been inflamed by hanging in speechless suspense on the throw of a die rather than refined by longing after the adventurous march of virtue in the pages of history.

The statesman, it is true, might with more propriety leave the faro bank or the card table to take the helm, for he still has only to shuffle and play tricks. The whole system of British politics, if it may courteously be called a system, consists in multiplying dependents and devising taxes that grind the poor to pamper the rich. So a war, or any wild-goose chase, is, as common people say, a lucky turn-up of patronage for the minister, whose chief merit is the art of keeping himself in office.

It is not necessary, then, that he should have any compassion for the poor, so long as he can secure the odd trick for his family. Or if some show of respect for what is called, with ignorant ostentation, an Englishman’s birthright should be useful for cheating the gruff mastiff that he has to lead by the nose, he can make an empty show quite safely by giving his own single vote and letting his light squadron of followers file off to the other side. And when a question of humanity is debated, he may dip a sop in the milk of human kindness to silence Cerberus, and talk of the interest his heart takes in an attempt to stop the earth crying for vengeance as it drinks in its children’s blood, even though his cold hand may at that very moment be riveting their chains by sanctioning the abominable slave trade. A minister remains a minister only so long as he can carry any point he is determined to carry. Yet it is not necessary for a minister to feel like a man, when a bold push might shake his seat.
But, to finish with these digressions, let me return to the more plausible slavery that chains the very soul of woman and keeps her forever in the bondage of ignorance.
